canberra.title: Woman who started fire that killed partner’s ‘beloved pet’ sentenced
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This story refers to suicide and family violence. A woman’s decision to start a fire in her then-partner’s h...
canberra.content:
Justice Belinda Baker said the fire was not “planned or premediated”, and the woman was “not acting out of revenge or to intimidate” another person. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This story refers to suicide and family violence.

A woman’s decision to start a fire in her then-partner’s home that killed his dog and destroyed personal items was “not planned nor premeditated”, a court has heard.

On Tuesday (21 July), ACT Supreme Court Justice Baker handed a woman a suspended sentence for setting the fire that destroyed a Canberra home.

Region has chosen not to name the offender to avoid identifying her partner.

On the day of the offending, the woman and her then-partner discussed their housing arrangements.

That night, the offender stayed downstairs to sleep on the couch while her partner went upstairs to bed.

The court heard the couple were in a relationship between October 2023 and May 2024, and were living at the victim’s home at the time of the offending.

The woman put a blanket over an oil heater with the intent of taking her own life, ultimately starting a blaze that quickly spread to the rest of the living room.

“It is accepted that she was reckless as to the spread of the fire,” Justice Baker said.

When the woman’s partner came downstairs, he picked up the heater, burning his hands, before unsuccessfully trying to smother the fire with a towel.

By the time ACT Fire and Rescue arrived, much of the house’s interior was alight, Justice Baker said.

The victim tried searching for his dog, but had to leave without finding the animal when the smoke began to affect his breathing.

He was taken to hospital with burns to his hands, feet and head, before being transferred to a Sydney hospital for specialised treatment.

He spent two weeks in hospital during his recovery.

On Tuesday, Justice Baker said the fire had significantly affected the victim’s physical and mental health.

She pointed to his victim impact statement, where he outlined how he has struggled to find work since the fire and that his injuries made it difficult for him to play a musical instrument.

“He feels unable to date other women … [He is] reliant on family and friends to perform daily tasks because he does not want to see or talk to anyone.”

She also said he described “the particular devastation” and guilt of being unable to save his “beloved pet” in the blaze, which had also destroyed sentimental items and certificates.

The court heard that the woman had a criminal history in NSW and the ACT, which included property damage.

Justice Baker said that the woman was receiving help to find longer-term housing interstate, and was also being supported by NDIS caseworkers.

Justice Baker said there was a “clear and direct connection” between the woman’s mental health and the offending, which reduced her moral culpability.

She accepted a submission from the woman’s lawyer that the woman’s expressions of remorse needed to be considered in light of her mental health diagnoses.

She said that when discussing the offending with the author of a pre-sentence report, the woman “became distressed” and “neither accepted nor denied responsibility”.

“However, the onus is on the offender to demonstrate remorse … [There is] no basis to make this finding in her favour.”

She found that while the only appropriate sentence would be one of imprisonment, the woman’s mental health struggles would make time in custody “particularly onerous”.

Justice Baker described her decisions that night as “not planned or premediated”.

The woman was ultimately convicted of an arson charge and handed a suspended 20-month prison sentence and a good behaviour order.

A separate charge of aggravated recklessly inflicting actual bodily harm (family violence) was also taken into account at sentencing.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 02 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 02 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

You can also submit an online report about a historical sexual assault allegation for incidents that occurred more than six months ago.

canberra.title: Is Telstra Tower being left to rot at the hands of vandals?
canberra.snippet: Regular visitors to Telstra Tower are beginning to express their concern about the condition and maintenance of the iconic building, with...
canberra.content:
Hikers and visitors to Black Mountain are beginning to express their concerns about the condition and maintenance of Telstra Tower. Photo: Michelle Kroll, Insert: Supplied.

Regular visitors to Telstra Tower are beginning to express their concern about the condition and maintenance of the iconic building, with reports of break-ins and vandalism at the site.

Telstra Tower closed its doors to the public in 2021, and despite a promise from the ACT Government and Telstra to refurbish the site in 2024, it has lain dormant ever since.

A regular hiker of Black Mountain, Kaydon Smit, said he was shocked to see the fencing around the tower left in such poor condition.

“It’s bloody disappointing walking past and seeing the state it’s in,” he said.

“It’s the most recognisable building in the ACT, you can see it from kilometres away, and yet when you stand at the base of the building, it looks like a rubbish heap.

“It’s been like this ever since the pandemic. It just feels like no one is taking any pride in restoring the tower at the moment.”

Life-long Canberran and architecture student Charles Pitcher said he is frustrated to see the iconic building left in such a condition. He said he believes more should be done to have the building operational again.

“As someone who’s lived in Canberra my whole life, I’d say Black Mountain Tower is more iconic than Parliament House,” he said.

“You can see it from almost anywhere in the city, and it’s the landmark that tells you you’re home – whether you’re driving back from Sydney, Jindabyne, or landing at Canberra Airport.

“I remember visiting once on a school maths excursion where we used Pythagoras’ theorem to calculate the distance to Springbank Island on Lake Burley Griffin.

“It’s a shame such an iconic landmark isn’t being better utilised.”

Telstra says graffiti at the site is removed as quickly as possible. Photo: Supplied.

Since April, ACT Policing has had two reports of people attempting to enter the site; however, no charges were laid.

Despite the graffiti and the trashed fences, Telstra said it is still committed to refurbishing the site and having it re-open to the public in the future.

“As soon as we became aware of the damage to the fencing, we removed the broken section and are arranging for it to be replaced and reinforced,” a spokesperson said.

“We’re also organising for the graffiti to be removed as quickly as possible. The tower continues to operate as an active telecommunications facility, so maintaining security is a priority.

“We know the site is an important landmark for the community, and we’re continuing to work closely with the ACT Government on plans to reopen the tower.”

In January, Telstra said it hopes to begin refurbishing the site by the end of 2027, with the aid of a $233,000 commitment from the ACT Government announced in June 2025.

“We want Telstra Tower to once again be part of a great Canberra tourism experience,” ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr said at the time.

“By working with Telstra to deliver a commercially viable and modern fit-out, we can secure the future of this iconic landmark and boost tourism activity.”

Telstra InfraCo CEO Brendon Riley echoed Mr Barr’s commitment.

“Telstra is proud to be partnering with the ACT Government to revitalise this iconic site,” he said.

“We’ve already taken important steps by preparing the tower for redevelopment, and we look forward to supporting the ACT’s vision through detailed design collaboration and a staged re-opening.

“This project represents a strong commitment from both parties to create something enduring for the Canberra community and its visitors.”

canberra.title: Israeli embassy offers public advice to ALP ahead of national conference
canberra.snippet: The Israeli embassy in Canberra has taken the unusual step of criticising a domestic policy platform, issuing a four-page media statement...
canberra.content:
The Embassy of Israel says Labor is placing too much blame on Israel over its conflict with Palestinian Photo: Yuliia Bukovska.

The Israeli embassy in Canberra has taken the unusual step of criticising a domestic policy platform, issuing a four-page media statement ahead of this week’s Labor Party National Conference.

The statement addresses Labor’s draft national position on Israel and Palestine, to be put to conference delegates, and which contains stronger language than has previously been used against Israel.

The draft platform opposes “settler violence” and Israel’s new death penalty laws, and supports the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

While the draft platform condemns Hamas, it doesn’t call for the Palestinian terrorist group’s disarmament.

Foreign embassies rarely engage publicly in the politics of their host nations, but Labor’s national conferences are only held every three years, and its platform on the Middle East could be significantly beefed up from what was adopted in 2023.

With that in mind, the Israeli embassy has moved to strongly criticise the draft platform ahead of the imminent conference.

It says the platform places too much responsibility on Israel over its conflict with Palestine.

“The Embassy of Israel notes these policy motions are still in draft form, and will continue to engage constructively with the Australian Labor Party through the usual diplomatic channels,” it states.

“However, the embassy respectfully submits that several elements of the draft national platform risk placing responsibility for the conflict on one party while giving insufficient attention to the decisions, conduct and continuing obligations of the Palestinian leadership and terrorist organisations such as Hamas.”

The statement says “settler violence” receives “disproportionate attention” and does not reflect the “identity or values” of the State of Israel.

“The government of Israel and the settler movement itself condemns it, and security forces work to apprehend these forms of illegal behaviour,” it states.

“It should be recognised that there is a significant amount of disinformation surrounding ‘settler violence’.

“The UN and others rely on false information in their description of it … Those seeking peace would be better served to focus their scrutiny on the terrorism experienced by both Jewish and Arab Israelis at the hands of terrorist groups such as Hamas.”

The lengthy statement concludes by urging all political parties to frame their policies “not around assigning blame”, but around promoting the “conditions that history demonstrates” are essential for lasting peace.

Those conditions include:

  • the recognition of Israel’s historic connection to the land and right to exist
  • the cessation of terrorism by all Palestinian organisations
  • the dismantling and disarmament of Hamas and other terrorist groups
  • an end to incitement and the glorification of terrorism, and
  • direct negotiations leading to a secure and enduring peace.

“Israel has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to make difficult compromises when genuine peace is possible,” the embassy said.

“It remains committed to a future in which Israelis and Palestinians live alongside one another in peace and security.

“That future, however, cannot be built through unilateral political declarations or international pressure directed at only one side.”

The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network (APAN) says that despite what the Israeli embassy might say, Labor’s platform is “totally insufficient” and “does not acknowledge the Palestinian genocide”.

APAN executive officer Katie Shammas said Labor’s conference will be a defining moment for the party.

“Labor cannot claim to champion human rights and international law while continuing policies that contribute to Israel’s violations,” she said in a recent statement.

“This conference is the moment Labor can choose to draw a clear red line on Australian complicity.

“That means ending defence exports that risk contributing to atrocities, confronting the illegal settlement enterprise, and ensuring Australia meets its obligations under international law.

“History will remember what Labor chose to do while Palestinians were being killed, starved and driven from their homes.”

APAN is calling on delegates to strengthen the national platform by committing to:

  • ending Australian defence exports and military cooperation that risk contributing to war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide
  • ensuring full transparency and accountability across Australia’s defence trade
  • taking concrete action against Israel’s illegal settlement enterprise, including ending Australian trade and investment that sustains it
  • divesting Future Fund investments linked to Israel’s occupation and illegal settlements, and
  • strengthening Australia’s commitment to accountability under international law for war crimes and other serious violations.

Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth, speaking to ABC Radio on Tuesday (20 July), said the government was not concerned about the Israeli embassy’s public intervention.

She also noted that the platform is yet to be debated.

“That’s entirely a matter for the Israeli embassy about what they will and won’t comment on,” the minister said.

“I can tell you that the national conference process is a very dynamic and exciting conference and our focus will be really on those key issues and putting a position and a platform that puts the Labor Party in a very good position.”

canberra.title: Man ‘essentially lost his temper’, pulled fake gun during road rage confrontation
canberra.snippet: A man has escaped jail time for pulling a “realistic-looking imitation” gun on a female driver during a road rage incident. D...
canberra.content:
21 July 2026

The court heard that Deane Richard Roach, 49, admits that he “got carried away” during the confrontation. Photo: Claire Sams.

A man has escaped jail time for pulling a “realistic-looking imitation” gun on a female driver during a road rage incident.

Deane Richard Roach, 49, faced the ACT Magistrates Court for sentencing on a charge of unauthorised possession or use of a prohibited firearm on Monday (20 July).

The court heard the incident started when the victim ‘brake-checked’ him and cut him off while they were driving.

His lawyer said that instead of reacting in the “more orthodox fashion” of yelling, Roach pulled out the fake firearm.

“[This was] he accepts, was an attempt to scare her … [Following this, she] disengaged and called the police,” the lawyer said.

He said there was a “degree of poetic justice” in how ACT Policing officers, armed with real firearms, ultimately took his client into custody.

In the aftermath, he said Roach was “compliant and cooperative” with police, telling them where the fake gun was located.

“He was upfront about having been agitated during the incident,” the lawyer said.

The court also heard that the gun wasn’t loaded.

Roach’s lawyer also told the court that his client felt “shame and regret” for his behaviour.

“He accepts that he got carried away,” he said.

He urged the court to impose a fully suspended sentence, arguing that Roach’s guilty plea, his remorse and his experience during his arrest were sufficient deterrents.

A prosecutor described the fake gun as a “black-coloured Glock” and said the incident had been a “very traumatic experience for the complainant”.

He asked the court to include “some form of community work” in Roach’s sentence.

Ultimately, Magistrate James Stewart handed Roach a suspended sentence.

He said the offending arose out of a “two-way display of very, very poor driving” before Roach pulled out the fake gun, which had a “very obvious resemblance” to a real weapon.

“It would seem that he, essentially, lost his temper … [He used the fake gun] in a very, very inappropriate way,” Magistrate Stewart said.

He described the offender as having “demonstrated true empathy and insight” into his offending, and said he had spent the year since the incident “working hard” to build a pro-social life.

“He’s a businessman. He’s striving to achieve his goals in Queanbeyan with a retail store.”

Roach was handed an 88-day prison sentence, which was immediately suspended and a 12-month good behaviour order.

He must also complete 37 hours of community service within 12 months.

canberra.title: $1.2 million Hellenic Club penalty facing recalculation amid ‘vague and uncertain’ gambling laws
canberra.snippet: The Hellenic Club has been “partially successful” in a bid to overturn a $1.2 million fine over allegations it improperly han...
canberra.content:
Hellenic Club at Woden has appealed its $1.2 million fine. Photo: Hellenic Club.

The Hellenic Club has been “partially successful” in a bid to overturn a $1.2 million fine over allegations it improperly handled problem gambling by two Canberrans.

In late 2024, the ACT Gambling and Racing Commission handed the Hellenic Club in Woden a $1.2 million fine and a reprimand over how it managed problem gambling by regular player Raimo Kasurinen (known as Ray).

He died by suicide on 31 March 2020, days after he and his wife had their Toyota LandCruiser repossessed.

The commission alleged that the club had failed to deal with 28 problem gambling incidents involving Mr Kasurinen or his wife between December 2017 and March 2023, including through its policy allowing people to make multiple $200 cash withdrawals using EFTPOS.

The Hellenic Club appealed to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal (ACAT), with Acting Presidential Member Greg Curtin SC and Senior Member Emma Morrison finding partly in its favour.

According to the decision, the Kasurinens became members of the club around 2008, and they would visit the venue about once or twice a week.

By about 2017, they were attending the Hellenic Club more often, with the club paying for their meals, offering preferential parking and listing Ms Kasurinen on an internal list of the ‘Club’s Top Twenty’ gamblers.

“Electronic records for carded play (when the member’s membership card was inserted in a gaming machine) reveal that the Kasurinens lost at least $345,000 on the gaming machines between October 2012 and February 2020,” the members state.

Mr Curtin and Ms Morrison found that, when looking at the 28 instances of alleged problem gambling, they accepted there was some understanding about the Kasurinens’ gambling.

“It is true that the club admitted that certain behaviours occurred which would fall within one of the problem gambling behaviours, it is true that the club admitted that some of those behaviours were known to someone in the club … But what was not present was evidence that any particular employee was aware of at least two of those behaviours and had the subjective opinion that those behaviours were signs of a gambling problem.”

They also noted no employees who gave evidence to the tribunal said they were aware of any signs of problem gambling by the couple.

“Unless that evidence of their subjective state of mind is rejected, then the problem gambling part of the case must be decided in favour of the club,” the members said.

“We do not consider that we should reject the evidence of those employees or former employees as to their subjective opinions at the time.”

ACAT heard the Kasurinens first joined the Hellenic Club in about 2008. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

However, Mr Curtin and Ms Morrison rejected the Hellenic Club’s argument around cash withdrawals made by Ms Kasurinen.

Under a legal limit, someone is blocked from withdrawing more than $200 in cash at a licensee’s premises under law.

Mr Curtin and Ms Morrison said that Mrs Kasurinen’s behaviour (when she would make multiple transactions) raised the question of whether those consecutive $200 withdrawals amounted to one transaction.

The Hellenic Club had argued that more than one withdrawal in a short period would still fall within the legal limits.

But the ACAT members said that the approach relied on an “artificial” difference.

“In the present case, Mrs Kasurinen’s multiple transactions occurred immediately consecutively and within seconds or a very small number of minutes, and it does not matter whether each transaction was completed in the way described by the club’s employees, or they happened as described by Mrs Kasurinen,” they said.

“In substance, on either version, they amounted to one act or action in withdrawing money and are therefore withdrawals for the purpose of [that withdrawal limit].”

The two ACAT members described the Kasurinens’ family members as having shown “dignity and grace” during the tribunal proceedings, and acknowledged their decision “probably [will] come as a disappointment”.

“We hope they understand that the result has arisen from vague and uncertain laws, with the Commission thinking those laws meant one thing whilst we have held that they meant another,” they said.

When contacted by Region, Hellenic Club CEO Ian Cameron said the club was pleased with the outcome.

“We welcome the Tribunal’s findings, which support the club’s longstanding position in relation to the allegations concerning problem gambling,” he said in a statement.

“Throughout this process, the club has maintained that it takes its responsibilities around responsible gambling seriously and has always sought to provide a safe and supportive environment for its members.”

A three-day hearing will be held in November 2026 to determine what changes will be made to the penalty.

If this story has raised any issues for you, you can contact Lifeline’s 24-hour crisis support line on 13 11 14 or the Gambling Helpline on 1800 858 858. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

australia.title: ‘A big job ahead of him’: world leaders congratulate Andy Burnham as he becomes Britain’s PM
australia.snippet: Beyond the diplomatic platitudes global media focuses on the ‘immense’ scale of the challenge he faces in the job UK politics live – late...
australia.content:
World leaders have warmly congratulated Andy Burnham on his entry into 10 Downing Street as Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade, but international media largely focused on the scale of the challenges awaiting him.

Emmanuel Macron, France’s president, said he hoped for a deeper relationship “in the service of our peoples, and by giving new momentum to the partnership between the UK and the EU” rekindled by Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who spoke with Burnham on Monday evening including about continued support for Ukraine, said Germany and the UK were close partners and he looked forward to working together.

The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said she looked forward to “strengthening the EU-UK partnership”. A “very good first discussion” had revealed a common commitment to “bringing the EU and UK closer and closer”, she later added.

Beyond the diplomatic platitudes, however, media coverage focused on Burnham’s regional persona – and the huge task awaiting him. France’s Public Sénat said the new prime minister came from “the working class of the north of England”.

He had managed to “build an image as an ‘everyman’, appearing without a tie, very often in a T-shirt”, the political TV channel said on its website, standing out as “a politician on the ground, close to everyday concerns”.

Italy’s Corriere della Sera said the UK was experiencing “profound unease, instability and social resentment” and “needs a push” forward, but Burnham’s nationalisation, state intervention and reindustrialisation plans suggested he saw the past as a model.

The UK “appears incapable of imagining and planning for the future and prefers to take refuge in a backward-looking Eden”, it argued, even though the pre-Thatcher years were marked by “energy rationing, rubbish in the streets and IMF bailouts”.

The Irish Times noted that Burnham may be “a breath of fresh air” but the challenges that brought down Starmer – “a budget unable to meet desperately needed demand in defence, housing, welfare, care for the aged, and training for the young” – remained.

The new prime minister, the paper said, would be “hamstrung by a commitment to abide by strict fiscal rules. His instinct may be to tack to the left, but he is already trying to prove that … he will govern from the centre” and the job was “immense”.

In an New York Times essay titled The King of the North Won’t Save Britain, Tom Hazeldine said that with his “northern accent, casual attire and everyman persona”, Burnham “trades on his outsider status, a precious commodity in antipolitical times”.

But, Hazeldine added, a UK that had wanted “a bounce” after Starmer had actually ended up with – in the absence of anything better – “a career Blairite with a northern soul and a Whitehall brain. For the country, it looks a lot like more of the same.”

Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, wished Burnham “a successful tenure”, adding that Italy and the UK were “bound by a deep friendship and a collaboration that, over the years, has grown ever stronger” and she was sure would continue.

Outside the EU, Donald Trump, who had previously described Burnham as “the mayor of a town” and “extremely liberal”, said on Monday night the two had had a “very good conversation” on topics including North Sea oil.

“The Prime Minister has got a big job ahead of him, but he will be able to do it and, of course, the U.S.A. will be there to help!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “The call was interesting, and went very well. I wished Prime Minister Burnham, GOOD LUCK AND GODSPEED!”

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, described the UK as “one of the global leaders”, adding that the two countries’ relationship was “stronger than ever and Kyiv stood “ready to work together in all possible formats”.

Anthony Albanese, the Australian prime minister, said Australia and the UK were “longstanding friends” bound by “deep ties”. He looked forward to strengthening the partnership and promoting “security, resilience and prosperity in the years ahead”.

australia.title: Hanson’s support for Trump deportation policy ‘makes me sick’, Monique Ryan says – as it happened
australia.snippet: Follow today’s news live Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Alpine ski resorts in New South Wales and Victoria ...
australia.content:
Monique Ryan condemns Pauline Hanson’s comments on deportations and White Australia policy

Independent MP Monique Ryan has condemned a number of recent comments by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Ryan called Hanson’s comments saying she admires Donald Trump’s approach to mass deportation makes her “sick”.

I’ve seen footage of people being killed during the process of deportation in the US. I’ve seen people being removed from hospital settings and medical clinics, the thought of that happening in this country makes me sick. The fact that Pauline Hanson thinks that’s a reasonable way to treat and deal with vulnerable people tells me that she is not fit to have any significant leadership role in the country.

Ryan also rejected Hanson’s accusation she was misinterpreted to appear as if she said that she supported a White Australia policy.

I think it would appear that One Nation doesn’t know what they believe. On one hand it does not talk to the other combine a bit doesn’t know what Pauline is saying, they are incredibly incoherent as a political force. It’s remarkable they are getting as much airtime as they are. The need to be held to account and come up with reasonable, rational policies if they really believe that they have any role to play in the leadership of this country.”

  • Qantas has apologised to about 250 passengers who were stuck on the tarmac in Sydney for four-and-a-half hours on Monday afternoon while the airline dealt with multiple separate problems.

  • A Melbourne synagogue was unsuccessful in applications for government grants for security before a December 2024 arson attack that has seen its doors closed ever since.

  • WA police have arrested a 16-year-old boy who allegedly stabbed his mother to death and allegedly turned the knife on his sister, who managed to flee to get help.

Thanks for joining us, see you bright and early tomorrow morning.

Krishani Dhanji

Wong presses for prosecutions over methanol poisonings in meeting with Lao counterpart

The foreign minister, Penny Wong, has pressed her Lao counterpart over a decision not to pursue the most serious charges in relation to the methanol poisoning deaths of Holly Bowles and Bianca Jones.

Wong met with her Lao counterpart Thongsavanh Phomvihane on the sidelines of the Asean foreign ministers meeting today in the Philippines.

The government has pushed for a transparent investigation into the death, and put further pressure on Laos to hold those responsible to account.

In a statement from Manila, Wong said the government would continue to pursue the matter with Lao officials.

I made clear that Australia expects the Lao Government to ensure this investigation fully reflects the seriousness of this tragedy and that those responsible are held properly to account.Our advocacy for Holly and Bianca’s families is not over.

Last week the government sent special envoy Pablo Kang to Laos to convey Australia’s objections to authorities on the ground.

Patrick Commins

Housing Australia Future Fund must be more transparent: auditor general

The government’s $10bn Housing Australia Future Fund has provided 1,432 of the 40,000 homes Labor promised would be built by the end of the decade, according to a new Australian National Audit Office report that criticised Treasury for not being transparent about the program’s performance.

The HAFF disburses a minimum of $500m a year to build social and affordable homes, and the ANAO judged that the design of the HAFF was “largely effective”.

But the independent audit office said that Treasury should do better in reporting on how the program was progressing against its own targets, as it noted that the average cost per home built under the HAFF was $770,387 over 25 years.

Experts and the government’s own Housing Australia do not expect the government to meet its ambitious home building target.

One of the ANAO’s five recommendations – all of which were accepted by the Treasury – was that the department “publicly and clearly reports on program performance, including the performance of sub-activities and programs, as well as the overall program”.

Clare O’Neil, the minister for housing and homelessness, in a statement said she welcomed the report. She said:

The auditor general has identified practical opportunities to strengthen governance, risk management and public reporting as the program continues to mature.

We welcome those recommendations and will continue improving the way the program is delivered.

Qld government considering investment in four pumped hydro projects

Queensland’s government is considering investing in just four pumped hydro projects, parliamentary estimates heard today.

The former Labor government planned to build two huge multi-billion dollar schemes, the $18.4bn Borumba scheme and the world’s largest project at Pioneer Burdekin, costing $36.8bn. In opposition, the LNP promised to cancel the latter and instead build multiple “smaller more manageable” projects, but with no additional details.

Queensland Investment Corporation CEO Kylie Rampa revealed in parliamentary estimates this evening that her agency was leading an assessment of four projects, known as “project gravity”.

It considered three projects to replace the 5,000 megawatt Pioneer Burdekin scheme, Big T, Capricornia and Mt Rawdon. The last project has already been rejected by the state government. The corporation is also considering the Borumba project. Rampa said:

We assess these projects using a consistent evaluation framework aligned with the energy roadmap objectives, projects were assessed against a comprehensive set of principles, including commercial outcomes, strategic fit, broader impacts and risks, deliverability and feasibility.

Monique Ryan raises concerns over AI datacentre locations, urges government protection

Independent MP Monique Ryan says she has concerns about where existing and future AI datacentres are built and has urged the government to ensure “there are protections in place”.

When asked whether she would want one in her electorate on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, she said:

I think people would be concerned. Sound pollution is an increasing concern for people. We have seen in states 75% of people are now saying they don’t want one in the area and there’s a good reason for that.

When asked where they should be placed, she said they should be near energy sources and “powered by 100% new renewables”. She said:

That should not be taking electricity out of our existing power supply. So companies building them can ensure 100% new renewables to them and water sovereignty as well.

Dead stranded baby whale returns negative bird flu test

A humpback whale calf that died on Greenhills Beach in Cronulla last week has tested negative for bird flu. It comes after responders were called to the stranding last Friday morning after a public report to ORRCA’s hotline.

The test was carried out under NSW’s H5 bird flu surveillance program, which can include marine mammals such as whales and seals.

Authorities say the newborn animal, confirmed to be just a few days old, most likely died from complications linked to a difficult or traumatic birth.

A spokesperson for the state’s Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development said:

Examination findings showed the calf was born alive and had taken its first breaths, with no evidence it had been able to feed from its mother.

While it is not possible to determine the exact events leading to the calf’s death, the findings indicate the animal experienced serious complications shortly before or during birth and was unable to survive in the critical first days of life.

The department said a full necropsy test “may take some weeks to come back.”

First Nations protesters rally at US military base in Northern Territory

Ben Doherty

Hundreds of protesters have marched towards the gates of the secretive US-run intelligence base Pine Gap, on Arrernte land on the outskirts of Mparntwe-Alice Springs, demanding it be shut down.

On Monday, traditional owners delivered a letter to the facility requesting the base be shuttered and the land it occupies returned to the Arrernte people.

Traditional owner Felicity Hayes said the base was the cause of sadness for her people, and should be the source of shame for Australia and the US.

We want our Apmere (land) back … My country is a sacred place … for me and my families and for everybody in Australia so today I wanted to tell them that we don’t want Pine Gap to ever exist on our land. Shut it down. Close it down and give our land back.

Pine Gap was established in 1966 by the CIA. It is, technically, a “joint facility” between Australia and the US, but it is always run by an American. Its precise role is shrouded in secrecy, but it is known to provide key surveillance and targeting information for US military operations. The information gathered by satellites and sent through Pine Gap has been linked to US and Israeli strikes in Gaza and elsewhere across the Middle East. The US military regards Pine Gap as one of its most valuable offshore intelligence assets.

On Tuesday morning, protester Aahana Nag locked herself to the steering wheel of a vehicle blocking Hatt Road, the main road into the base. She was arrested and taken into custody by NT police. Nag said, in a statement:

The United States has displaced the custodians of these lands and has built an intelligence facility that provides critical intelligence for their illegal military operations.

How can we allow this when the United States is currently conducting illegal attacks and invasions globally?

Nag said Australia should end its military alliance with the US.

This base is material proof of the federal government’s investment in US wars that do not serve us.

Family rejects coroner’s newborn death finding

A family whose daughter died hours after her birth from an undiagnosed heart defect has rejected a coroner’s finding that the baby’s death was not preventable, AAP reports.

Thea Flaskett died on the morning of 11 September 2023, a little more than four hours after she was born at a Queensland hospital. Thea’s parents Meg and James Flaskett had fought for an inquest into their daughter’s death, which held hearings in Brisbane in 2025.

Meg Flaskett said the family was “devastated but not surprised by the outcome” in a statement that criticised the inquest’s findings. She disputed that Thea’s heart defect was the only major contributor to her death at Redcliffe hospital, north of Brisbane. She said:

Had Thea’s condition been diagnosed before birth, her labour, delivery and immediate management would have been fundamentally different.

Although these findings bring the coronial process to an end, they do not bring us peace, nor do they answer the questions that have driven us for almost three years.

Luca Ittimani

New KPMG CEO was on executive during ‘botched’ inaction on leaks, Labor inquiry chair says

Labor senator Deb O’Neill has taken aim at KPMG’s new CEO in connection to the firm’s failure to confirm or address leaks in its audit team.

John Sams, today appointed chief executive, is a KPMG lifer who had been the firm’s chief financial officer and a board member since October.

O’Neill, the chair of a parliamentary inquiry, said in a public statement:

Mr Sams’ appointment is the elevation of yet another member of the firm’s leadership which oversaw the series of botched investigations and non-action.

The inquiry has heard KPMG’s board’s subcommittee commissioned legal advice which found no evidence for the leak allegations in December. Only after the allegations were publicly revealed in March did KPMG re-investigate, verify and act on some of the allegations. KPMG declined to comment. Sams did not sit on the subcommittee.

O’Neill previously took aim at KPMG when it replaced its outgoing chair with Michael Ebeid, an internal independent director who had oversight of last year’s investigation. She took another shot at Ebeid in her comments today.

Ebeid is yet to officially become chair but still sat on the selection panel that today appointed Sams. The firm’s 680 partners have to vote on whether to change their partnership agreement so Ebeid can serve as independent chair. O’Neill said:

I note reports of concerns within KPMG about the role Mr Ebeid has played in advancing the path of Mr Sams to CEO, given there has been no formal agreement by partners to allow Mr Ebeid, who is not a partner of KPMG, to assume the role of Chair of the Board.

Contacted on behalf of Ebeid and Sams, KPMG declined to comment. Ebeid today said Sams was also endorsed by the board.

Andrew Messenger

Tamworth sports journalist killed in rural car accident

A well-known sports journalist has been reportedly killed in a car accident while travelling from a football competition.

Tamworth writer Mark Bode, 57, has been named as the driver killed in a three vehicle crash on the Oxley Highway near Somerton at about 6.30pm on Saturday. The small town is about halfway between Gunnedah and Tamworth.

His paper, the Northern Daily Leader, reports that he was travelling home from a rugby league competition in Gunnedah.

A 69-year-old man in the other vehicle was also treated at the scene before being airlifted to John Hunter hospital in a serious condition.

Both occupants of the third vehicle were uninjured.

Bode spent decades in regional journalism after starting his career in Brisbane. He joined the Leader in 2017 and is being remembered as a passionate and hard-working sports reporter, best known for his profiles of local athletes.

Perth teenager arrested after allegedly stabbing mother to death, injuring sister

A 16-year-old boy has allegedly stabbed his own mother to death and turned the knife on his little sister who managed to flee to get help, AAP reports.

Police attended a home in the suburb of Bentley, in Perth’s south-east, after the incident which authorities say occurred at about 6:15am on Tuesday.

Officers located the body of the 35-year-old mother inside the family’s Mill Street home, Acting Insp Jessica Securo told reporters.

The girl was also stabbed but managed to flee the house, making it to a nearby highway for help. Securo said:

I can confirm there is no ongoing risk to the wider community.

This incident will have a significant impact on the family, friends and loved ones of all those involved as well as the broader community.

Our thoughts are with them all, particularly the 12-year-old girl who remains in hospital receiving treatment. We ask that their privacy be respected during this investigation.

Penry Buckley

Jewish schools council says poorer schools using education funding for security

Stephen Rothman, a former NSW supreme court judge who is the co-chair Australian Council of Jewish Schools (ACJS), the representative body for schools throughout the country, has been explaining to the royal commission on antisemitism how Jewish schools are funded, including security costs.

Rothman has said since 2023, “the level of vitriolic antisemitic abuse has been significant, and in my view, normalised to such an extent that members of the community generally feel unwelcome and unprotected”.

ACJS analysis shows the national total for security spending in the four years to 2022 to 2025 is more than $58m. Rothman said be believes every Jewish independent school funds this through levies to parents, but this is “normally significantly lower” than poorer schools needs to spend in relation to security per student, with schools drawing on their own funds or from increased fees to cover costs.

It’s a somewhat tongue-in-cheek line by members of the Jewish community that it’s expensive to be Jewish, and it is, a lot of money is spent on donations and the like, it’s part of the culture, but nevertheless, if you can get the donations, yes, that’s good. If you can’t get the donations … [schools] will use resources that other schools would use for all sorts of other facilities to fund security, including education, unfortunately.

Rothman said the ACJS’s position is “at least the recurrent expenditure on guards and other operational … expenditures” should be funded by the federal government.

Ima Caldwell

Now the wonderful Achol Arok will take you through the rest of today’s breaking news.

Penry Buckley

Jewish school has looked at diverting school funding to meet security needs

The royal commission on antisemitism on social cohesion has been hearing about the security burden on Jewish schools in Sydney and Melbourne following a rise in antisemitic incidents sine October 2023.

Before lunch, it heard from Mount Scopus Memorial College and Bialik College in Melbourne, which like many independent Jewish schools, charge parents security levies in addition to fees, which have increased significantly since October 2023. They described antisemitic incidents directed at students.

This afternoon, Linda Emms, the principal of Emanuel School in Sydney, has said while the majority of its security costs came from levies charged to parents, they did not fully cover increasing costs, meaning “over the last 18 months in my time at the school, it has meant that we’ve had to look at diverting funds from other areas of school operations”.

She said the start of the 2026 school year, had brought an “added layer of complexity” for Emanuel, which is near Bondi beach, with many staff, student and parents impacted by the terror attack in December. Emms said the school has a police presence every day.

Our parents have worked incredibly hard, particularly with some of our younger students, to get their children to see the police as their friends and as being there to protect them.And I watch some of them come in, and they will fist bump the police as they come in of a morning and say hello to them. And it’s lovely, but it’s really sad that we have parents who actually have to do this, because that’s how they’re actually reassuring their child that it’s OK that there’s actually police at the front gate every morning.

Andrew Messenger

Queensland police ethical standards investigating after man dies in Brisbane city watch house

The Queensland police ethical standards unit is investigating the death of a man at the Brisbane city watch house yesterday.

The 55-year-old Thornlands man had been in the facility since Friday. He was arrested that day, 17 July, at about 10.50am on a return to prison warrant.

He told staff he was feeling unwell on Monday shortly after 3pm and was assessed by nursing staff and other emergency services. He died a short time later. His cause of death is under investigation.

The Queensland police ethical standards command is investigating the death in custody on behalf of the state coroner. The state’s watch houses are operated by Queensland police and are designed for adult detainees to be held for about 48 hours.

There are 72 people currently being held in the Brisbane watch house; eight of them have been there longer than a week, one for 12 days.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Kumanjayi Little Baby review exposes failures; Gaza celebrates Spain’s World Cup win; and the case for nude saunas
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

Kumanjayi Little Baby’s mother was “effectively” left alone to protect her children while also experiencing domestic violence, a draft review tabled in the NT parliament has found, because child protection authorities failed to adequately assess multiple threats to her safety.

But despite those conclusions, the interim report, tabled in the Northern Territory parliament on Tuesday, was unable to draw a link between the child protection referrals and the five-year-old Warlpiri girl’s death.

The child, known after her death as Kumanjayi Little Baby for cultural reasons, was allegedly abducted and murdered in April by Jefferson Lewis, a man unknown to her or her family.

Top news

  • Nine to axe 30 jobs at the Age and SMH due to ‘extreme’ AI disruption

  • ‘Disturbing parallels’: Holocaust survivors president says exclusion of Jews from public life similar to Nazi Germany

  • Climate and rock art advocates take on Woodside’s ‘carbon bomb’ WA gas project in federal court

  • Nicaragua’s president says country will not hold any more elections

  • Israel criticises Labor’s draft Palestine policy in rare foreign intervention ahead of party conference

  • Man, 28, charged with murder of former UK MP Ann Widdecombe

  • Almost 90 football fields of woody habitat were bulldozed every day in NSW – despite pledges to rein it in

In video

The Spanish football team’s World Cup win has been celebrated in the streets of Gaza, where Spain’s support for Palestinian rights and Israel’s backing for the Argentinian team turned the competition into more than a football showdown. Gathered at cafes and outdoor screenings, Palestinians defied the risk of Israeli attacks to cheer on a team they had taken to their hearts.

What they said …

“I think – sit down!” – Barnaby Joyce

In a moment that has gone quickly viral online, the former Nationals turned One Nation MP startled viewers when he bellowed at his dog offscreen during an interview with ABC’s 7.30 program.

Full Story

Burnham begins: what awaits the new British PM?

Andy Burnham has finally realised his long-held ambition to become prime minister. But what problems can he expect to confront now he’s in No 10?

Senior political correspondent Peter Walker and former No 10 press secretary Paul Harrison analyse Andy Burnham’s first day as PM.

Listen to the episode here

Before bed read

Australians are becoming increasingly enthusiastic about saunas, with local Google searches for the term almost tripling in a month and sauna chains popping up across the nation.

But Kate Hennessy writes, Australians should be free to sweat it out in the nude – instead of being confined to swimwear.

australia.title: NSW doctor barred from practising for six months after operating on wrong end of patient’s bowel
australia.snippet: Dr Liu-Ming Schmidt found guilty of professional misconduct after tribunal considered complaints about her treatment of 13 patients Get o...
australia.content:
A surgeon has been found guilty of professional misconduct and barred from practising medicine for six months after she failed to detect cancer in one patient and operated on the wrong end of the bowel of another.

The New South Wales civil and administrative tribunal considered the treatment of 13 patients by Dr Liu-Ming Schmidt, finding her management of them fell significantly below reasonable standards.

The tribunal found Schmidt “made a catastrophic error” when she operated on the wrong end of a 79-year-old man’s bowel. He had been transferred to Albury hospital in December 2019, and was found through a CT scan to have a perforated bowel, requiring a section of the bowel to be removed.

He also needed a stoma, where an opening on the abdomen is created by the surgeon so a colostomy bag can be connected for waste removal.

Schmidt “brought out the wrong end of the bowel when she formed the stoma,” the tribunal decision said. “She caused a complete mechanical bowel obstruction so that the stoma was not capable of passing faecal material.”

The tribunal found Schmidt’s “conduct of the procedure was significantly below the relevant standard”.

A coronial inquest into the 79-year-old’s death, referred to in the tribunal’s decision, found he died as a result of complications of inflammation, which was contributed to by the surgical error made by Schmidt.

“Other contributing causes to his physical decline and death included the prolonged delay in diagnosis of a mechanical bowel obstruction together with underlying natural causes,” the decision said.

The tribunal found Schmidt also failed to provide the man with appropriate post-operative care.

In another patient, Schmidt failed to perform a complete colonoscopy and because of this, did not detect a cancer that the tribunal found should have been identified during the procedure.

During the hearing, Schmidt said she had addressed the concerns raised and had engaged in self-reflection, further education, re-certification and education from peers.

“She has maintained and developed professional relationships and is constantly auditing, reflecting, analysing and discussing her performance,” the tribunal decision said.

The tribunal heard there were five patients where Schmidt failed to take the adequate time to perform colonoscopies. The procedure in one patient was finished in five minutes. Schmidt admitted to the tribunal she did not take enough time for the procedures.

She also failed to adequately capture images during the procedure in several patients, the tribunal found.

An expert witness who reviewed the cases told the tribunal that his main concern regarding those patients was “the relatively rapid time taken by Dr Schmidt to conduct the colonoscopies”.

“A rapid withdrawal time, he said, will lead to lesions being missed,” the decision said. Lesions found during a colonoscopy may indicate cancer.

In 2023, an investigation was launched by the Health Care Complaints Commission (HCCC) and Medical Council of New South Wales after a panel of experts reviewed patients Schmidt had treated between 2018 and 2022.

At the time, almost 2,000 patients who received colonoscopies performed or supervised by Schmidt were told they may need to have their procedures repeated to ensure they do not have cancer.

The tribunal found that of these, about 1,000 underwent a repeat colonoscopy. Seven of them were diagnosed with cancer.

“No one has, nor could they, say that this was a result of a failure by Dr Schmidt to identify a problem with the original colonoscopy,” the decision said.

“However, Dr Schmidt’s explanation to us for doing colonoscopies in a much shorter time than the standard, is that, as a surgeon with 10 years’ experience, she has been doing colonoscopies in the way she was taught in her training. She says this is confirmed by being regularly reaccredited after submitting all of the relevant information to the authorities.

“We cannot accept this explanation. The evidence before us is to the effect that Dr Schmidt’s training would have informed her that she needed to take longer than she had been taking to do a colonoscopy to ensure thoroughness in checking for abnormalities.”

Dr Schmidt admitted to the tribunal that her conduct was sufficiently serious to justify suspension or cancellation of her registration.

Once her suspension expires, Schmidt will have a number of conditions on her registration, including being required to practise under supervision.

australia.title: Man of his word: Pope Leo speeches declared human-authored by Australian AI detection tool
australia.snippet: Maps of Hope has been certified by Proudly Human, a company led by former chief scientist, Dr Alan Finkel Follow our Australia news live ...
australia.content:
A collection of speeches and writings by Pope Leo XIV has been certified as human-authored less than two months after Leo declared artificial intelligence the greatest threat to humanity.

Proudly Human, the Australian company spearheaded by Australia’s former chief scientist, Dr Alan Finkel, undertook a review of a collection of writings and speeches by the pope, in collaboration with the publisher, the Australian Catholic University and cardinals in the Vatican.

Maps of Hope was published in the same week in May that Leo’s first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, warned of the dangers of artificial intelligence and the risks of the power of the technology being concentrated in the hands of a few.

In the encyclical, Leo said AI should be prevented “from dominating humanity,” adding that the technology should be “human-friendly”, accessible to all and open to discussion and debate.

Finkel told Guardian Australia he had a “great deal of confidence” going into the Maps of Hope process that Leo’s speeches would be human-written by a human, and within a day, Proudly Human had certified the collection as human-created.

The process typically requires authors or their representatives to sign up to the site, go through an ID check, and sign a declaration that they are operating within minimum standards: AI can’t be used to write the first draft, or write sentences and paragraphs.

The company then uses AI detection tools that Finkel said “focus on different nuances” in writing and grammar.

“We use a suite of four or five of them and our own averaging algorithm, and we test that suite every night to make sure that they’re really continuously fit for purpose,” he said. “In this case, the book came through, as you would expect, is basically purely human.”

The terms and conditions for the service outline that certifications are made “on the basis of information” provided and the checks performed, and the certifications can be refused or revoked if found to misrepresent authorship or “fall outside our published standards”.

Finkel’s hope is that in lieu of government regulation forcing authors to disclose AI use, people can use the information to know whether writing was produced by a human.

“They deserve to know. I actually think it’s a fundamental right [for] human beings,” he said, adding this was particularly true when it came to religious figures.

“If you’re sitting in a church and you’re expecting that that is the genuine expertise, religious wisdom, of the priest who’s delivering the sermon.

“The heart of what it is to be human is to engage with other people and to exchange ideas and exchange creative ideas.”

The president and vice-chancellor of the Australian Catholic University, Prof Zlato Skrbis, said in a statement that given there was so much online content being generated so quickly, it was valuable to “say with confidence that a work is a product of human reflection and judgment”.

world.title: Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds
world.snippet: Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy...
world.content:
One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability.

There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned.

Global hunger declined for a third consecutive year in 2025, with 7.8% of people affected, down from 8.1% in 2024. There were also signs that a prolonged upward trend in Africa was coming to a halt.

However, the proportion of people who cannot afford a healthy diet remains “extremely high”, said Maximo Torero, chief economist of the Food and Agriculture Organization, one of the report’s authors.

The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report calculated the cost of a healthy diet is 4.28 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars a day. This means that in any given country, a healthy diet costs the amount of local currency with the same buying power that $4.28 has in the US.

“The extreme poverty line is $3PPP per person,” Torero said. “So it’s significantly higher.”

He said government policies had typically focused on subsidising cereals and starchy staples, rather than meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables.

“That means calories, but not a diversity of diet,” he said, highlighting the impact of this on rates of obesity and diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Figures from the World Health Organization, another of the UN agencies behind the report, show adult obesity rose from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024.

“It’s extremely urgent,” Torero said. “Obesity [among adults] is growing at a very steep level, so we need to now work intensively on trying to minimise those risks and those hidden costs that that substantial increase in obesity will bring.”

He called for investment in infrastructure, research and development. Modelling in the report suggests more efficient supply chains could bring down the costs of meat and dairy as well as fruit and vegetables. New policies to encourage greater consumption of fruit and vegetables could also pay dividends, he suggested, reducing the economic impact of health issues linked to poor diets.

In Africa, 66.6% of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet in 2025, more than double the levels observed in Asia or Latin America and the Caribbean.

Africa is now home to the highest number of hungry people for the first time, with about 309 million, surpassing Asia’s 292 million, the report showed.

The rise is largely driven by higher population growth on the continent, Torero said, with the proportion of the population going hungry actually starting to decrease “for the first time in years”.

“I think this is extremely important, because the numbers are for 2025, where already we have seen a significant reduction in overseas development assistance in the region,” Torero said.

Shipping restrictions in the strait of Hormuz linked to the conflict in the Middle East are likely to hit next year’s figures, he said.

The report is authored by the FAO, WHO, Unicef, the UN World Food Programme and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.

world.title: São Tomé and Príncipe heads to polls in tense presidential election
world.snippet: Incumbent Carlos Vila Nova hopes to defeat his former party and secure second term as independent Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to t...
world.content:
Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to the polls for a presidential election on Sunday as one of Africa’s least populous countries seeks to burnish its democratic credentials.

According to the National Election Commission, about 142,000 people are registered to vote in the tiny African state’s elections, approximately 15% of whom live in the diaspora.

Since gaining independence from Portugal in 1975, the island country off Africa’s west coast has built a solid reputation for peaceful, competitive elections. But this year’s vote comes amid a tense political atmosphere and a lingering constitutional crisis.

The president, Carlos Vila Nova, is running for a second term as an independent, rather than as the candidate for the ruling Acção Democrática Independente (ADI), whom he represented when he was elected in 2021.

The tensions between Vila Nova and his former party began in January last year when he dismissed the prime minister, Patrice Trovoada. Trovoada’s replacement, the former justice minister Ilza Amado Vaz, resigned after just three days, before the current holder, Américo Ramos, took office.

On Sunday, Vila Nova will be running against four other candidates including the ADI parliamentary leader, Nito D’Abreu. Another former prime minister, Jorge Bom Jesus, attempted to withdraw his independent candidacy, but missed the deadline and remains on the ballot.

The main opposition party, the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, is now part of a broad coalition backing the incumbent president, despite being staunch ADI opponents. Meanwhile, an ADI faction led by Ramos is backing D’Abreu. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the election will go on to a second round.

The businessman Domingos Monteiro, known as “Nino”, who has been president of the São Toméan Football Federation since 2015, was disqualified after the constitutional court ruled he did not meet the eligibility requirements. Monteiro was born on the island, but his parents never became naturalised citizens after moving from Cape Verde where they were born.

“The constitutional court is violating the principle of equal rights … It is time for descendants born in São Tomé and Príncipe to say no to discrimination, to the culture of xenophobia and persecution,” said Monteiro.

For voters, priorities include tackling government corruption, high inflation, severe youth unemployment, chronic fuel shortages, and frequent blackouts. Rivals of Vila Nova are hoping this will keep him from a second term and propel them to the presidency.

Corruption in São Tomé and Príncipe “is the greatest catastrophe the country has experienced in this half-century [of independence”, D’Abreu said at the presidential debate on Tuesday.

The country is seen as a trusted western ally for security and maritime trade in the Gulf of Guinea, one of the world’s biggest maritime piracy hotspots. It also has offshore oil deposits that make a significant contribution to its economy. Observer missions from the European Union, G7+ and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries are on the ground to monitor the polls.

world.title: ‘We are preserving a tradition’: how Ghana’s sensationalist film posters became collectible art
world.snippet: Hand-painted works are often wildly unfaithful to the movies they portray – reinterpretations that sometimes resulted in threats, insults...
world.content:
Sitting on his porch in Teshie near Accra, Heavy J dipped a brush into red oil paint and dabbed it carefully on to his canvas – a flour sack – adding blood to a knife being wielded by a man. Higher on the canvas, he had started on an outline of a skull.

Heavy J was creating a poster, but not as you might have expected for a horror film. Instead, it was for the animated fairytale The Little Mermaid. The man with the knife was not a killer but the film’s kind-hearted prince, Eric. The skull was also unrelated to the story. “We add more to make people interested,” said Heavy J, whose real name is Jeaurs Affutu.

Hand-painted film posters by local artists were a hallmark of Ghanaian film culture from the late 1970s to the early 2000s, used to advertise screenings for neighbourhood venues known as video clubs after organisers realised that the original posters were not attracting enough audiences.

Plot lines were regarded as little more than jump-off points for humorous and surreal flights of fancy. Artists working for different video clubs competed to make the best “forgery”, as they described their interpretations.

The practice began to wane around the turn of the century as more Ghanaians gained access to electricity and their own TV sets and video players. Many video clubs went out of business and painters pivoted to create other work. But by then the posters had attained global interest, popularised in books and foreign exhibitions, and old and rare paintings became prized collectibles.

There was a lull in interest in newly painted posters in the early part of the 21st century, but demand has risen, driven by online marketing and a receptive customer base of film lovers in the west.

Deadly Prey Gallery has been working with artists to preserve the culture of making hand-painted film posters, while helping meet the increased demand.

Named after an action film, the business was co-founded in 2012 by Brian Chankin, then a video rental store owner in Chicago, and Robert Kofi, a Ghanaian who, as a child, used to work as a “hype man” for video centres in his home town of Winneba and later started collecting and selling posters. They partnered after Kofi sold Chankin some works.

Deadly Prey Gallery works with 15 artists, including Heavy J, who has been painting posters for four decades, connecting them to online customers and shipping the artwork on completion.

Most orders come from the US. Old action, science fiction and horror films have the highest demand. Popular titles include The Exorcist and the Star Wars and Terminator franchises. And prices for commissioned pieces start at $600 (£450) and vary based on the canvas size and other customer preferences.

Kofi, who is based in Accra, is part manager and part editor. He identifies the artists most suited for each work, shares his vision of the posters with them and makes regular visits to their workspaces to review works in progress.

In a studio in Ashaiman, about 11 miles from Heavy J’s house, another artist called Stoger was working on two commissions: one for the horror film Poltergeist, and another for the experimental drama Gummo, which contains multiple acts of violence against cats and a scene in which a character eats spaghetti in a bath tub.

The poster showed three cats and a man in a bath with a plate of spaghetti in front of him. In his feedback that day, Kofi, speaking in Ga, a primary language of Ghana, told Stoger two of the cats were not aggressive enough and the food was too clean. “I want uglier cat scenes,” he later explained. “The spaghetti has to be dirtier.”

Stoger, born Benjamin Amartey, was a sculptor before developing an interest in films and becoming a poster painter in 1992. “I use my imagination to make scenes that will attract people so that they’ll love the poster,” he said.

The emphasis on exaggeration comes from an African tradition of “visualising the invisible”, said Joseph Oduro-Frimpong, the director of the Centre of African Popular Culture at Ashesi University and a poster collector himself.

“The posters’ audiences have not seen the film, so it’s impossible for them to know [whether they are accurate]. Therefore, the artists tap into what they call imaginative painting,” he said. “They will highlight these things and in doing so they incorporate things that are not in there. There is a kind of sensationalism to it.”

The reinterpretations at times resulted in threats, insults and even physical attacks from viewers who felt duped. Kofi laughed when he recalled an incident in the 1990s when people beat him up after they watched the action film Double Impact and realised it did not have a scene showing Jean-Claude Van Damme carrying out a beheading, as was illustrated on the poster.

At the Centre for National Culture in Accra, dozens of colourful posters from Deadly Prey Gallery are pinned on wooden walls. They include Jennifer Lopez launching an arrow at a snake in Anaconda, and a mouse coming out of Jamie Lee Curtis’ mouth in Halloween.

“We are preserving a tradition,” Kofi said of the poster-painting craft. “We are preserving a history.”

world.title: Seven Americans quarantining at Kenya Ebola facility after US travel ban, says aid group
world.snippet: Aid workers are first known people to quarantine at facility, which sparked huge opposition in Kenya Seven American aid workers who had b...
world.content:
Seven American aid workers who had been in Congo to fight the Ebola outbreak are quarantining at a new isolation facility in ⁠Kenya after the US government introduced travel ⁠restrictions, the head of a US charity ​employing them told Reuters.

The aid workers are the first known people to quarantine at the facility, which has sparked huge opposition in Kenya and is at the heart of a legal case in which a court has ordered the work to be ⁠suspended. Construction continued, however, according to US officials and satellite imagery reviewed by Reuters.

Washington’s new policy says American citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where there is an Ebola outbreak, must spend three weeks in a third country before entering the United States.

The US government is building ⁠the 50-bed bio-isolation unit on an air force base in central Kenya for asymptomatic Americans exposed to the virus in Democratic Republic of the Congo or Uganda. Many Kenyans are angered at what ​they see as the US offloading the health risk such patients pose.

Last month, Kenya’s ‌health minister announced an immediate halt to the facility’s ‌construction after he was found in contempt of court for failing to observe the order to halt work pending a final ruling.

“Samaritan’s Purse has seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team staff ‌members there,” Franklin Graham, president and CEO of Samaritan’s Purse, told Reuters in response to questions.

“None of them have any symptoms, but they are being quarantined by the Kenyan government for 21 days,” Graham said.

A US state department official told Reuters a group of asymptomatic Americans who had served on the frontlines of the Ebola response had “voluntarily moved to the Kenya facility for precautionary monitoring and isolation”.

“Kenyan authorities have authorized their movement into the facility under the observation of the US public health service clinicians,” the official said, adding that the decision was taken “strictly out of an abundance of caution”.

Kenyan health ministry officials did not immediately respond to calls or requests for comment ‌on the move. A senior Kenyan foreign ministry official said they had no information on it.

Another source familiar with the matter who asked for anonymity said that the group had arrived at the site in central Kenya on Monday and were sleeping in army cots in tents.

He said some ​had treated Ebola patients at the Christian aid group’s treatment centres in Congo but others had carried out work such as construction, with no direct contact with the sick.

“There is one potential high-risk exposure,” he said, adding that their health was being monitored. Kenyan authorities are not allowing the group to leave the facility to travel anywhere else in the country, he added.

The often fatal viral disease spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids from infected people or animals.

Samaritan’s Purse, which has been promised several million dollars from the Trump administration for the ⁠Ebola response, is an evangelical Christian group that works in disaster zones around the world.

It is one of the biggest foreign ​aid groups treating Ebola in Congo and has the largest number of ​Americans there, working closely alongside the World Health Organization to ​contain the outbreak. One of its US staff members who caught Ebola earlier this month was transferred to a hospital in Germany on Monday.

world.title: UK aid cuts ‘reduce bilateral support to some African countries by 90%’
world.snippet: Critics say Foreign Office figures send ‘global message about the role the country wants to play on international stage’ Labour’s foreign...
world.content:
Labour’s foreign aid cuts mean reductions of as much as 90% in the bilateral support the UK will give to some African countries, Foreign Office figures show.

The department’s annual report includes a long-awaited breakdown of how the reduction in the aid budget will affect individual countries for the next three years.

Analysis by Bond, the umbrella group for development charities, shows cuts of 90% for Mozambique and Malawi by 2029, 80% for Rwanda and Sierra Leone and 49% for Somalia.

Bond’s chief executive, Romilly Greenhill, said: “By slashing UK aid funding to countries like Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Uganda, this Labour government is abandoning communities on the frontlines of conflict and the climate crisis and risks plunging these countries’ populations into poverty and instability.”

Keir Starmer’s government announced deep reductions to spending on overseas aid last year to fund increases in the defence budget, prompting the resignation of Anneliese Dodds as development minister.

Part of Labour’s approach in implementing the cuts has been to switch its focus to funding multilateral donors such as the World Bank, which it argues is a more efficient use of straitened resources.

Explaining the cuts in a written statement to parliament in March, the foreign secretary, Yvette Cooper, said: “In a range of countries, we will transition away from spending high levels of grant ODA [overseas development assistance], but our ambition and effort will remain high – delivering through modernised partnerships, and making the most of what the UK has to offer.”

Charities, however, say the scale of the reduction in direct support to individual countries will jeopardise vital projects.

The director of global outcomes at Save the Children, Lisa Wise, said: “Today’s international budget allocations reflect what we already know – reductions in public investment in countries and children that need it most. These choices send a global message about the role the UK wants to play on the international stage.”

The next steps for Labour’s development policy will fall to the incoming prime minister Andy Burnham’s pick for foreign secretary. The current energy secretary, Ed Miliband, is seen as a likely contender for the role.

Some MPs have urged Burnham to act to restore the party’s leadership on development, including by setting a path back towards the target of spending 0.7% of national income on overseas aid.

The UK takes on the chair of the G20 next year – the coordinating body that includes China, India and Brazil alongside wealthy countries in the global north.

Greenhill urged the new PM and foreign secretary to use that role “to champion the global reforms needed to address poverty and inequality among the world’s marginalised communities”.

The development minister, Jenny Chapman, said: “The world has changed. Crises in one part of the world now affect us all.

“Just this year, conflict in the Middle East has driven up food and fertiliser costs and the Ebola outbreak that began in the DRC is an urgent reminder why global health security matters.

“We’re not turning away from these challenges. We’re making every pound of UK development spending work harder, for people facing the toughest crises and for taxpayers at home.”
